export function useTelegramAccountQuery(pollMs?: number) {

    queryKey: qk.telegramAccount,
    queryFn: () => getTelegramAccount(),

  });

// that completes it when opened.
export function useStartTelegramLink() {
  return useMutation({ mutationFn: () => startTelegramLink() });
}

  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: () => unlinkTelegramAccount(),
    onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.telegramAccount }),
  });
}

// How to name a connected account: the @username when Telegram has one, otherwise
// the first name, otherwise a plain statement that it is connected.
export function useTelegramAccountLabel() {
  const t = useTranslations('account.accounts');
  return (link: { username: string | null; firstName: string | null }) =>
    link.username ? `@${link.username}` : (link.firstName ?? t('telegramConnectedLabel'));
}

FILE: apps/web/src/services/views.service.test.ts
================================================
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { describe, it } from 'node:test';
import type { View } from '@/lib/api/endpoints/views';
import { movedInRow } from './views.service';

function view(id: number, flags: Partial<View> = {}): View {
  return {
    id,
    projectId: 1,
    name: `V${id}`,
    icon: null,
    filters: { conditions: [] },
    display: { layout: 'kanban' } as View['display'],
    position: id,
    shareToken: null,
    shareExtended: false,
    shareExpiresAt: null,
    isPrivate: false,
    favorite: false,
    hidden: false,
    createdAt: '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z',
    ...flags,
  };
}

const ids = (views: View[] | null) => views?.map((v) => v.id);

describe('movedInRow', () => {
  // A favorite and a private view in the middle of the caller's row.
  const row = [view(1), view(2, { favorite: true }), view(3, { isPrivate: true }), view(4)];

  it('moves the view to the place of the one it is dropped on, over favorites and private ones', () => {
    assert.deepEqual(ids(movedInRow(row, 4, 2)), [1, 4, 2, 3]);
    assert.deepEqual(ids(movedInRow(row, 1, 3)), [2, 3, 1, 4]);
  });

  it('moves to the front of the row for a drop on All', () => {
    assert.deepEqual(ids(movedInRow(row, 3, null)), [3, 1, 2, 4]);
  });

  it('keeps a hidden view between the same neighbours', () => {
    const withHidden = [view(1), view(2, { hidden: true }), view(3), view(4)];
    assert.deepEqual(ids(movedInRow(withHidden, 4, 1)), [4, 1, 2, 3]);
  });

  it('moves nothing when the view stays where it is', () => {
    assert.equal(movedInRow(row, 1, null), null);
    assert.equal(movedInRow(row, 2, 2), null);
    assert.equal(movedInRow(row, 9, 1), null);
  });
});

import { useMutation, useQuery, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useTranslations } from 'next-intl';
import { toast } from 'sonner';
import {
  type View,
  listViews,
  createView,
  updateView,
  deleteView,
  setViewFavorite,
  publishView,
  setViewHidden,
  arrangeTabRow,
  resetTabRow,
  reorderViews,
} from '@/lib/api/endpoints/views';
import { EMPTY_FILTER_SET, type FilterSet } from '@/utils/filters';
import { normalizeSavedDisplay } from '@/utils/viewSettings';
import { useOptimisticReorder } from '@/services/optimisticReorder';
import { qk } from '@/services/queryKeys';

// Coerces a view's jsonb blobs (opaque on the server) into the client shapes,
// filling defaults for a missing/partial display or filter set. Applied by the
// views query and after a create/update so consumers always get client shapes.
export function normalizeView(v: View): View {
  const conditions = (v.filters as FilterSet | undefined)?.conditions;
  return {
    ...v,
    filters: Array.isArray(conditions) ? { conditions } : EMPTY_FILTER_SET,
    display: normalizeSavedDisplay(v.display),
  };
}

// The caller's tab row with the dragged view moved to the target's place, or to the
// front for a null target; null when nothing moves.
export function movedInRow(row: View[], draggedId: number, targetId: number | null): View[] | null {
  const from = row.findIndex((v) => v.id === draggedId);
  const to = targetId == null ? 0 : row.findIndex((v) => v.id === targetId);
  if (from < 0 || to < 0 || from === to) return null;
  const next = [...row];
  const [moved] = next.splice(from, 1);
  next.splice(to, 0, moved);
  return next;
}

export function useViewsQuery(projectKey: string | null) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: qk.views(projectKey ?? ''),
    queryFn: () => listViews(projectKey!),
    enabled: projectKey != null,
    // The server answers in the order of the caller's own tab row.
    select: (rows) => rows.map(normalizeView),
  });
}

      createView(projectKey!, input),
    onSuccess: () => {
      if (projectKey) void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.views(projectKey) });
    },
  });
}

      updateView(id, input),

      if (projectKey) void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.views(projectKey) });
    },
  });
}

}

}

// Sets the project's order, which applies to the views a person has not placed in their own
// row. The caller's own row keeps its order, so the cache waits for the server instead of
// moving the project's views ahead of it.
export function useReorderViews(projectKey: string | null) {
  const t = useTranslations('views');
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: (orderedIds: number[]) => reorderViews(projectKey!, orderedIds),
    onSuccess: () => {
      toast.success(t('projectOrderSet'));
      if (projectKey) void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.views(projectKey) });
    },
  });
}

import { keepPreviousData, useMutation, useQuery, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import {
  addWorkspaceAdmin,
  createWorkspaceScimToken,
  deleteWorkspace,
  getWorkspace,
  getWorkspaceScim,
  listWorkspaceManagerCandidates,
  listWorkspaceManagers,
  listWorkspaceProjectOptions,
  listWorkspaceScimGroups,
  listWorkspaces,
  removeWorkspaceAdmin,
  setWorkspaceScimGroupMappings,
  updateWorkspace,
  type WorkspacePatch,
  updateWorkspaceScim,
} from '@/lib/api/endpoints/workspaces';
import { qk } from '@/services/queryKeys';

export function useWorkspacesQuery() {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: qk.workspaces, queryFn: () => listWorkspaces() });
}

export function useWorkspaceQuery(workspaceId: number) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: qk.workspace(workspaceId),
    queryFn: () => getWorkspace(workspaceId),
  });
}

export function useUpdateWorkspace(workspaceId: number) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: (patch: WorkspacePatch) => updateWorkspace(workspaceId, patch),
    onSuccess: (workspace) => {
      qc.setQueryData(qk.workspace(workspaceId), workspace);
      void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.workspaces });
    },
  });
}

// Its teams go with it, so the team list changes as well as the workspace list.
export function useDeleteWorkspace(workspaceId: number) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: () => deleteWorkspace(workspaceId),
    onSuccess: () => {
      qc.removeQueries({ queryKey: qk.workspace(workspaceId) });
      void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.workspaces });
      void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.teams });
    },
  });
}

export function useWorkspaceManagersQuery(workspaceId: number) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: qk.workspaceManagers(workspaceId),
    queryFn: () => listWorkspaceManagers(workspaceId),
  });
}

export function useWorkspaceManagerCandidatesQuery(workspaceId: number, search: string) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: qk.workspaceManagerCandidates(workspaceId, search),
    queryFn: () => listWorkspaceManagerCandidates(workspaceId, search),
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
  });
}

// The manager list, the candidates and the counter on the workspace all change with it.
function useManagerMutation<T>(workspaceId: number, write: (userId: string) => Promise<T>) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: write,
    onSuccess: () => void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.workspace(workspaceId) }),
  });
}

export function useAddWorkspaceAdmin(workspaceId: number) {
  return useManagerMutation(workspaceId, (userId) => addWorkspaceAdmin(workspaceId, userId));
}

export function useRemoveWorkspaceAdmin(workspaceId: number) {
  return useManagerMutation(workspaceId, (userId) => removeWorkspaceAdmin(workspaceId, userId));
}

// SCIM provisioning: the token an identity provider authenticates with, and what the
// groups it pushes grant. A workspace's, or the instance's in god mode for null.
export function useWorkspaceScimQuery(workspaceId: number | null) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: qk.scim(workspaceId),
    queryFn: () => getWorkspaceScim(workspaceId),
  });
}

export function useUpdateWorkspaceScim(workspaceId: number | null) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: (patch: { enabled: boolean }) => updateWorkspaceScim(workspaceId, patch),
    onSuccess: (data) => qc.setQueryData(qk.scim(workspaceId), data),
  });
}

export function useCreateWorkspaceScimToken(workspaceId: number | null) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: () => createWorkspaceScimToken(workspaceId),
    // The response is the token itself, not the settings, so the redacted view has
    // to be refetched for its new prefix.
    onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.scim(workspaceId), exact: true }),
  });
}

export function useWorkspaceScimGroupsQuery(workspaceId: number | null) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: qk.scimGroups(workspaceId),
    queryFn: () => listWorkspaceScimGroups(workspaceId),
  });
}

export function useSetWorkspaceScimGroupMappings(workspaceId: number | null) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: (input: {
      groupId: string;
      mappings: { projectId: number; role: 'owner' | 'member'; roleId: number | null }[];
    }) => setWorkspaceScimGroupMappings(workspaceId, input.groupId, input.mappings),
    onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: qk.scimGroups(workspaceId) }),
  });
}

// Every project a group may grant, for the group mapping picker.
export function useWorkspaceProjectOptionsQuery(workspaceId: number | null) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: qk.scimProjects(workspaceId),
    queryFn: () => listWorkspaceProjectOptions(workspaceId),
  });
}

# worker

Standalone Bun process (own Dockerfile). `start.ts` runs three poll loops: `worker.ts` (webhook and
notification delivery, webhook cleanup, telemetry), `agent-worker.ts` (cron schedules) and
`import-worker.ts` (source imports). Intervals, batch sizes, leases and attempts come from the job
settings in `@repo/db`, read on every pass. The import pipeline: `docs/dev/import-worker.md`.

## Invariants

- **Reads and writes `@repo/db` directly, never the API over HTTP.** It does not import `apps/api`.
- **No migrations here.** Compose and Helm apply them in a separate step and the worker waits. On
  Railway and a plain `docker run` the api applies them at startup, so the worker can start first.
- **A DB error is retried and can use up attempts.** `poll-loop.ts` logs a failed claim and the next
  tick retries. During a notification send or an import phase the error goes only to `last_error`
  and counts as an attempt.
- **Queued webhooks are at-least-once.** `event_id` is set at enqueue and sent in
  `X-Itsaplan-Event-Id`, so receivers deduplicate. Never mint a new id per attempt. Notifications
  have no `event_id`: a retry can send a duplicate.
- **The worker queues cron schedules and runs no agent.** A due `cron` schedule of an active
  project gets an `agent_run` row. The api queues the other runs and executes internal agents. A
  runner or an invocation endpoint executes external ones.
- **Claims use a lease; `status` stays `pending`.** A claim pushes `next_attempt_at` forward by the
  webhook or notification lease of the job settings, or `LEASE_SECONDS` in `import-store.ts`. Cron
  schedules use a row lock in a transaction instead.
- **The webhook timeout is a socket idle timeout.** God mode refuses a lease that is not longer than
  it, but a receiver that keeps sending bytes can still outlast the lease.
- **Notification credentials are read, never taken from the caller.** A delivery row names its
  project; credentials come from the owning team and the instance config.
- **Always send a supplied URL through `pinnedFetch` from `@repo/net`, the SSRF guard.** That covers
  webhook URLs, import source hosts and attachment links.
- **Pure logic stays free of `@repo/db`.** `backoff.ts`, `reader.ts`, `*-adapter.ts` and
  `*-mapping.ts` import nothing from it, so unit tests run without a database.
- **An import job's credential is decrypted here, never routed through
  `packages/db/src/domains/`.** Only the worker decrypts it.
- A new import source needs a `SourceReader` adapter, an entry in `import-sources.ts`, api routes
  and a web form. The phases do not change. Rewrite makes no requests to the source.
- **Only `AttachmentRejectedError` is logged and skipped.** Any other attachment error fails the
  tick, an SSRF refusal (`UrlNotAllowedError`) included. `MAX_ATTEMPTS` failed ticks in a row fail
  the job (`import-retry.ts`).

## Tests

`src/__tests__/unit/` covers pure logic with no database. `src/__tests__/integration/` runs against
the test DB, and `import-store.test.ts` also uses the S3 test store. These tests insert the rows the
api writes in production; there is no api to call.

# itsaplan Helm Chart

Helm chart for deploying [It's a Plan](https://github.com/croffasia/itsaplan) on Kubernetes.

## Prerequisites

- Kubernetes 1.24+
- Helm 3.10+
- The published container images from `ghcr.io/croffasia/itsaplan-{api,web,worker,bot}`

## Quick start

```bash
helm install itsaplan charts/itsaplan \
  --set api.env.API_URL=https://api.example.com \
  --set api.env.APP_URL=https://app.example.com \
  --set api.env.S3_BUCKET=planner-attachments \
  --set secrets.postgresPassword=changeme \
  --set secrets.betterAuthSecret=$(openssl rand -base64 32) \
  --set secrets.appEncryptionKey=$(openssl rand -base64 32) \
  --set secrets.s3AccessKeyId=minioadmin \
  --set secrets.s3SecretAccessKey=minioadmin
```

This deploys the full stack with the built-in PostgreSQL and RustFS. For production, use a values file instead of `--set`
flags and store secrets externally (Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, etc.).

## What gets deployed

| Resource          | Kind                        | Condition                              |
|-------------------|-----------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| API (Elysia)      | Deployment + Service        | always                                 |
| Web (Next.js)     | Deployment + Service        | always                                 |
| Worker            | Deployment                  | always                                 |
| Bot (Telegram)    | Deployment                  | `bot.enabled` (default `true`)         |
| PostgreSQL        | StatefulSet + Service + PVC | `postgresql.enabled` (default `true`)  |
| RustFS            | Deployment + Service + PVC  | `minio.enabled` (default `true`)       |
| RustFS bucket init | Job (Helm hook)            | `minio.enabled`                        |
| Web Ingress       | Ingress                     | `ingress.enabled`                      |
| API Ingress       | Ingress or IngressRoute     | `ingress.enabled` + `ingress.api.mode` |
| TLS Certificate   | Certificate (cert-manager)  | `certificate.enabled`                  |
| ServiceAccount    | ServiceAccount              | `serviceAccount.create`                |

## Using an external database

Disable the built-in PostgreSQL and provide a connection string:

```yaml
postgresql:
  enabled: false

externalDatabase:
  url: "postgres://user:password@db.example.com:5432/itsaplan"
```

## Using an external S3-compatible store

Disable the built-in RustFS and provide an endpoint:

```yaml
minio:
  enabled: false

externalS3:
  endpoint: "https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com"

api:
  env:
    S3_BUCKET: "my-bucket"
    S3_REGION: "us-east-1"
    S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE: "false"  # false for AWS/R2, true for RustFS

secrets:
  s3AccessKeyId: "AKIA..."
  s3SecretAccessKey: "..."
```

## Ingress

Ingress is disabled by default. Enable it and choose how the API is exposed.

The API cannot serve behind a path prefix: better-auth mounts at `/api/auth/*`
and treats a path inside `API_URL` as a replacement for its base path. The chart offers two modes instead.

### Separate host (default mode)

The web and API each get their own hostname. Works with any ingress controller.

```yaml
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  host: app.example.com
  tls:
    enabled: true
    secretName: app-tls
  api:
    mode: separate-host
    host: api.example.com
    tls:
      enabled: true
      secretName: api-tls
```

### Traefik entrypoint

The API shares the web hostname but is served on a dedicated Traefik entrypoint (a separate port). Requires Traefik and
the `IngressRoute` CRD.

```yaml
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: traefik
  host: app.example.com
  tls:
    enabled: true
    secretName: app-tls
  api:
    mode: traefik-entrypoint
    entryPoint: apisecure
    publicPort: 8443
    tls:
      enabled: true
      secretName: app-tls
```

## TLS with cert-manager

If cert-manager is installed, the chart can create a Certificate resource:

```yaml
certificate:
  enabled: true
  issuerName: letsencrypt-prod
  issuerKind: ClusterIssuer
  dnsNames:
    - app.example.com
    - api.example.com
```

The generated secret is named `<release>-itsaplan-tls`. Reference it in
`ingress.tls.secretName` and `ingress.api.tls.secretName`.

## Disabling the Telegram bot

```yaml
bot:
  enabled: false
```

## Pro edition

`values-pro.yaml` runs the Pro images. Pass it before your own values file:

```bash
helm install itsaplan charts/itsaplan -f charts/itsaplan/values-pro.yaml -f values.yaml
```

Without a valid license the Pro images run as the core does. The license key is entered in
god mode, under **License**.

# Self-hosting

Requirements: Docker and a domain behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy.

The TLS proxy is required. In production the session cookie is marked `Secure`, and
browsers do not keep a `Secure` cookie that arrives over plain HTTP: over `http://` the sign-in
request succeeds, but no session is kept and the app stays signed out. `http://localhost` is the
one exception in Chrome and Firefox; WebKit browsers such as Safari refuse it there too.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/croffasia/itsaplan.git
cd itsaplan
cp .env.example .env
# fill in the eight values below
docker compose up -d
```

The stack refuses to start while one of these is missing:

| Variable                | Value                                      |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `API_URL`               | public URL of the api                      |
| `APP_URL`               | public origin of the web app               |
| `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`     | `openssl rand -base64 32`                  |
| `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`    | `openssl rand -base64 32`                  |
| `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`    | `openssl rand -base64 32`                  |
| `S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID`      | the RustFS root user, any name over 3 chars |
| `S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`  | `openssl rand -base64 32`                  |

On a machine with [Bun](https://bun.sh), the setup script generates them instead. Run
`bun install && bun run setup`, answer **Generate env**, and answer no when it offers to
write the files: it prints `.env` and `apps/web/.env` for you to copy onto the server.

That starts the whole stack: Postgres, RustFS, api, worker, bot, and web. The four services
run from the images published on each release. `VERSION` in `.env` pins one release instead
of the newest. The `migrate` service applies migrations before the api starts, and the first account you register
becomes the instance admin.

For the Pro edition, start the stack with `docker compose -f docker-compose.pro.yml up -d`.
It takes the same `.env` and runs the Pro images. Without a valid license they run as the core
does; the license key is entered in god mode, under **License**. The project name and the
volumes are those of `docker-compose.yml`, so an existing instance moves to Pro on the same
data. [Fast Deploy](https://itsaplan.dev/pro#fast-deploy) in your Pro account installs this
stack with Caddy for HTTPS on a new server in your Hetzner, Vultr or DigitalOcean account.

`.env.example` documents every variable, including the optional ones: legal document URLs,
passkey and cookie settings, telemetry opt-out, and worker tuning.

## Where the api lives

`API_URL` takes one of two forms:

- **Its own subdomain**, such as `https://api.example.com` beside `APP_URL=https://app.example.com`.
  The session cookie is set on the parent domain (`.example.com`), so every subdomain of it
  receives the cookie. `COOKIE_DOMAIN` narrows it when the two share a deeper parent. An
  `APP_URL` on the apex domain (`https://example.com`) has no parent to take, so this form
  needs `COOKIE_DOMAIN=.example.com`.
- **A path on the web's host**, such as `https://app.example.com/api` beside
  `APP_URL=https://app.example.com`. No second hostname or certificate is needed, and the
  session cookie stays on that one host: it has no `Domain`, and over HTTPS its name carries
  the `__Host-` prefix, which keeps another subdomain from setting one in its place.

With a path, the reverse proxy sends that path to the api and removes it on the way, so the
api receives `/projects`, `/api/auth/...` and `/mcp` as it does on its own subdomain:

```
https://app.example.com/api/*  ->  api:3000/*   (prefix removed)
https://app.example.com/*      ->  web:3001/*
```

For MCP clients that sign in with OAuth, the proxy also sends the discovery documents of the
host to the api: `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server*`,
`/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource*` and `/.well-known/openid-configuration*`.

MCP clients sign in with OAuth only over HTTPS. On an `API_URL` that is plain HTTP and not
`localhost`, MCP takes personal API keys only.

An authorization the api cannot hand back to the client, because it does not know the client
or its redirect URI, ends on the web's sign-in page, which says what happened. A client that
keeps a registration the instance no longer has is told to remove the server and add it again.

The OAuth redirect URIs that god mode shows include the path. An api on a different
registrable domain than the web app (`api.other.com`) does not work: the session cookie
cannot be shared across sites.

### Git webhooks on a private instance

GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo and Bitbucket deliver repository webhooks to
`<API_URL>/webhooks/git/<id>`. When `API_URL` is reachable only over a VPN or a private
network, expose that one route on a public hostname at the reverse proxy and set
`GIT_WEBHOOK_BASE_URL` to its origin:

```
GIT_WEBHOOK_BASE_URL=https://hooks.example.com
https://hooks.example.com/webhooks/git/*  ->  api:3000/webhooks/git/*
```

It changes only the payload URL: the settings page shows it, and the webhooks the instance
manages through a provider connection are created with it. A connected repository's existing
webhook is updated in place on the next reconcile: saving the provider token again, or
regenerating the project's webhook secret. Deliveries are still authenticated by the
project's secret. Auth, email links, the browser and MCP keep using `API_URL`.

### Client IP

The api rate-limits authentication per client address: sign-in, sign-up, password change and
email change to 3 requests per 10 seconds, sign-in links (requesting and opening one) to 5 per
minute, password reset and confirmation emails to 3 per minute. Change these numbers in god mode
under **Authentication → Request limits**; each is at least 1. Each api replica counts on its
own. It reads the address from `X-Forwarded-For` and takes it only when the header holds
one address. When it finds no address it can use, every client shares one limit per route,
and the api logs `Rate limiting could not determine a client IP` once.

Caddy, Traefik, and ingress-nginx in its default configuration drop the `X-Forwarded-For` a
client sends and write the address they see, so they need no setting. These setups do:

- **nginx** writes no `X-Forwarded-For` unless told to. Set
  `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;`. The common
  `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` appends the address to the one the client sent; with it, list
  the nginx address in `TRUSTED_PROXIES`.
- **Cloudflare** in front of the proxy: set `CLIENT_IP_HEADER=cf-connecting-ip`. Cloudflare
  puts the client address in that header, and the proxy behind it sees only Cloudflare's.
  The proxy must then accept connections from Cloudflare alone: a request sent to it directly
  carries any value in that header.
- **A chain of proxies that append**: list their addresses or CIDR ranges, comma-separated,
  in `TRUSTED_PROXIES`. The chain is read from the right, the listed addresses are skipped,
  and the first other one is the client.

`CLIENT_IP_HEADER` names any header the proxy writes itself, such as `x-real-ip` when nginx
sets `proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;`. A header the proxy passes on unchanged lets a
client pick its own address: Caddy passes `X-Real-IP` on as the client sent it.

A client that reaches the api without the proxy writes any of these headers itself.
`docker-compose.yml` publishes the api on `API_PORT` of the host; keep that port closed to
everything but the proxy.

### API key rate limit

One API key may send 1200 requests a minute. Each MCP message, such as a tool call, is one request. Change the limit
in god mode under **General → API keys**; 0 turns it off. A key over the limit gets HTTP 429
with a `Retry-After` header that says how many seconds remain in its minute. Each key has its
own count, and with several api replicas each replica counts on its own. A new limit applies at
once on the replica that saved it and within a minute on the others.

## Mail

The instance sends password resets, address confirmations, sign-in links and invites through
the mail provider set in god mode under **Integrations → Email provider**: SMTP or Resend.

A Microsoft 365 mailbox refuses a password over SMTP once it has MFA. Set **Authentication**
to **Microsoft 365 (OAuth)** instead: the instance signs in as an Entra ID app registration
and sends as the mailbox over XOAUTH2. An empty server is filled with
`smtp.office365.com:587` and STARTTLS. On the Microsoft side:

1. Register an app in Entra ID, add a client secret, and grant it the Office 365 Exchange
   Online application permission `SMTP.SendAsApp`, with admin consent.
2. In Exchange Online PowerShell, register the app's service principal and give it access
   to the mailbox: `New-ServicePrincipal -AppId <client id> -ObjectId <enterprise app object id>`,
   then `Add-MailboxPermission -Identity <mailbox> -User <service principal id> -AccessRights FullAccess`.
3. Turn on SMTP AUTH for that mailbox (`Set-CASMailbox <mailbox> -SmtpClientAuthenticationDisabled $false`).

Then paste the tenant ID, the client ID and the secret into the page and send a test. A
refused token is reported as rejected credentials and is not retried.

## Push notifications

Members can get their notifications as Web Push, next to email and Telegram, in each browser
they turn it on in: Chrome, Edge and Firefox, Safari on macOS, and Safari on iOS and iPadOS
16.4 or later once the app is added to the Home Screen. Push needs three variables, set on the
api and on the worker:

| Variable                     | Value                                                       |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `WEB_PUSH_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`  | from `bun run web-push:keys`                                |
| `WEB_PUSH_VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY` | from `bun run web-push:keys`; a secret                      |
| `WEB_PUSH_SUBJECT`           | a `mailto:` or `https:` contact the push services can reach |

While any of them is unset, push is off and the app does not offer it. Generate the key pair
once: a new pair ends every existing subscription, and members turn push on again in each
browser. The worker sends to the browsers' push services (Google, Mozilla, Apple), so it needs
outbound HTTPS. [docs/dev/web-push.md](dev/web-push.md) describes the whole path.

## Single sign-on

Any provider with an OpenID Connect discovery document works: Keycloak, Authentik, KanIDM,
GitLab, Forgejo, Okta, Entra. The credentials go into the database, not into `.env`, so
nothing here needs a restart.

1. In god mode, open **Integrations → Auth provider** and copy the redirect URI it shows
   (`<API_URL>/api/auth/oauth2/callback/oidc`).
2. Create a confidential client at your provider with that redirect URI.
3. Paste the discovery URL (`.../.well-known/openid-configuration`), the client ID and the
   client secret back into the page. Name the sign-in button and turn the provider on.

The first sign-in creates the account, and the registration mode under **Authentication**
decides whether it may: `open` creates it, `invite only` needs a pending invite that has
not expired, `closed` refuses it. Invites expire after the days set under **Authentication**
(7 by default, 0 for never); an expired one is renewed from the member list under a new
link. A refused sign-in returns to the sign-in page, which says why: the instance is
closed, it needs an invite, or the invite expired. On a closed instance, provision people
with SCIM.

A sign-in whose address already has an account joins that account instead of creating a
second one. That needs the provider to report the address as verified and the account to
have confirmed its own, so it is refused when the OIDC client leaves `email_verified` off
the token, or when the instance has no mail provider and so no confirmed accounts.
**Authentication → Trust addresses from sign-in providers** drops both conditions. Turn it
on only where you control who can register at the provider: anyone who registers an address
there takes over the account that holds it here.

Once a provider works, you can turn off **Authentication → Email and password**. The sign-in
and sign-up forms, password reset and sign-in links are then hidden and refused, and the
provider is the only way in. Passkeys keep working, because a passkey can only be added to an
account that already exists. The switch stays disabled until a provider is configured, so an
instance cannot be left with no way in.

## Provisioning with SCIM

An identity provider can create, deactivate and delete the accounts of the instance over
SCIM 2.0, and grant project access through its groups. Provisioning is set up in god mode by
the instance owner.

1. In god mode, open **SCIM**, generate a token and copy it — it is shown once — then turn
   provisioning on.
2. Point your provider's SCIM application at the endpoint the page shows
   (`<API_URL>/scim/v2`), authenticating with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
3. Push users, and groups if you use them.

The provider sees every account of the instance except those of AI agents. A create for an
address that already has an account links that account instead of making a second one, and a
name or address the provider sends is written to the account. While provisioning is on, the
provider decides which accounts are active, and god mode cannot deactivate or reactivate one.

Deactivating someone at the provider (`active: false`) keeps their teams and projects, but the
account cannot sign in, and its sessions and API keys are refused until it is reactivated.
Reactivating gives them the projects their groups grant. Deleting someone deletes the
account. The delete is refused while they are the only owner of a project outside their own
workspaces: deactivate them instead, or hand the project to another owner first. The instance
owner is outside SCIM's reach, and a repeated create for an address the provider already
linked answers "already exists" rather than overwriting the link.

A pushed group grants nothing until you say what it is for: on the same page, open a group
and add the projects its members should join, and the role they join on. A project belongs
to a team, so joining one also makes the person a member of that team, on the plain member
rank; the roles you can pick from are the team's. Removing a project from that list takes
away the memberships the group gave it, and once the group grants nothing else in that team,
the team membership goes with them. A membership someone got through an invite is never
touched by a sync, in either direction, and one the sync created cannot be edited from the
project's members page, nor ended from the team's — it changes at the identity provider.
What the person ranks as in the team is still the team's own to set.

A group also appears here without any explicit push, in two cases: a SCIM user whose
payload embeds a `groups` attribute instead of being assigned through a separate group
push, and anyone who signs in through OIDC while their identity provider puts a `groups`
claim on the token — set that up as a claim mapping on the OIDC client if the provider
supports one. Either way, map the group the same way once it shows up.

## Updating

```bash
git pull
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
```

`git pull` updates the compose file. The services come from the registry. Changing `API_URL`
or `APP_URL` afterwards only needs `docker compose up -d`.

The one-shot `migrate` service applies the migrations on every `docker compose up -d`, and
api, worker and bot start only after it succeeds, so an upgrade needs no database step.
Before it applies anything it dumps the database into the `db-backups` volume (`/backups`
in the `migrate` container) and fails if that dump fails — a release whose migrations
rewrite data is not applied without something to go back to. Dumps are deleted after 30
days, on the first startup past that; `BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS` changes the window and
`SKIP_PRE_MIGRATION_BACKUP=1` upgrades without one, for an operator who backs up by
other means. After the upgrade the app shows the instance owner where the dump is and
what the migrations changed.

Attachments are stored in RustFS. An instance set up with MinIO switches to it on the next
`docker compose up -d`: the `minio` service keeps its name and its `minio-data` volume, and
RustFS reads the files MinIO wrote in place, with the same credentials. Nothing is copied,
and the files stay readable by MinIO. The upgrade touches no attachment data, but a copy of
the volume before it costs one command:

```bash
docker run --rm -v itsaplan_minio-data:/data -v "$PWD":/out alpine tar czf /out/minio-data.tgz -C /data .
```

If you call the API from your own scripts or from an MCP client, read the
[release notes](https://github.com/croffasia/itsaplan/releases) for the paths a release removed.

## Building from source instead

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
```

That builds every service from this checkout and runs those images. Nothing else changes, and
the same command picks up local edits.

For a Coolify instance, see [coolify.md](coolify.md). For Kubernetes, see [helm.md](helm.md).
For a hosted deploy without a server of your own, see [railway.md](railway.md).

# @repo/auth: how it works

The rules are in `packages/auth/AGENTS.md`.

- `src/index.ts` builds the better-auth instance in `createAuth()`, with the Drizzle adapter
  (`provider: "pg"`) over `@repo/db`. `auth` is a proxy that calls `createAuth()` on first use.
  Email+password is enabled (`autoSignIn: true`; whether the address has to be confirmed first
  is an instance setting, see below).
- The plugins are passkey (`@better-auth/passkey`), API key, magic link, username, the instance
  OIDC provider, `jwt()` and `mcp()` (HTTPS or a loopback host only), and `openAPI()`.
- `emailAndPassword.revokeSessionsOnPasswordReset` is `true`: a reset ends every session of that
  account, since a reset is how a stolen password is dealt with. The signed-in change-password
  form in the web app sends `revokeOtherSessions` for the same reason. Neither touches personal
  API keys or an MCP client's refresh tokens.

## User role

The user table has a `role` column (`"god"` | `"user"`), declared as a better-auth
`additionalField` with `input: false` (not client-settable). A `databaseHooks.user.create.before`
hook sets it: the first user to register gets `"god"`, everyone after gets `"user"`.

`databaseHooks.user.create.after` calls `ensurePersonalWorkspace`, which gives an account that
owns no workspace one named after the person: the `"god"` account always, every other account
while `personalWorkspaces` is on in the auth settings. `authContext` in apps/api calls the same
function on every authenticated planner request, and an MCP tool call reaches a planner route.
So an account made by SCIM (a direct insert, which passes no hook), made while the setting was
off, or left with no workspace after deleting or handing over its own gets one on its next such
request, while the setting is on. `/me` does not pass through `authContext`. An agent's bot user
never gets one.

Each process keeps a set of accounts that need nothing (`settled`), so for them a request costs
no query. `forgetPersonalWorkspace` removes an account from the set in that process only. With
the setting off, a non-god account outside the set reads `app_setting` on each request.

`lastSeenAt` is another `additionalField`, with `input: false` and `returned: false`, so
better-auth leaves it out of a cookie session's response. A user loaded for an API key or an MCP
token still holds it, and the `/me` response leaves it out. apps/api writes it in the same
`authContext` step, at most once an hour per account, whether the request came with a session,
an API key or an MCP OAuth token. `/me` writes nothing. god's users list shows it as "Last seen".
Sessions are deleted on sign-out, so they are no record of when someone last used the app.

## Instance settings (`src/instance.ts`)

Registration mode, which sign-in methods are offered, the mail provider, the OAuth credentials
and the SCIM token are stored in the database, so god mode can change them without a restart.
The mail From address falls back to env (`EMAIL_FROM`, then `NOTIFICATIONS_EMAIL_FROM`).

- `app_setting` key `auth` → `{ registration, requireEmailVerification, magicLink,
  emailPassword, trustProviderEmails, personalWorkspaces, inviteTtlDays, inviteSearch,
  allowedEmailDomains, signInRateLimit, emailRateLimit, magicLinkRateLimit }`.
- `app_secret` keys `auth.email`, `auth.google`, `auth.oidc` and `auth.scim` → the mail
  provider, Google, the OIDC provider and the instance's SCIM token, set in god mode.
- `app_secret` key `workspace.<id>.scim` → a workspace's SCIM token, set by the workspace owner.
  Those routes answer 403 unless a build turns per-workspace SCIM on.

Each secret is encrypted with `@repo/crypto` and has a `redacted` mirror. The settings routes
decrypt the value and build their DTO from it. `workspacesWithOwnScim` and the worker's telemetry
read the mirror, which needs no key. No route returns a stored secret. A new SCIM token is
returned once, by the request that generates it.

The mail provider is read by the api and the worker as well, so its shape and reader are in
`@repo/db` (`domains/instance-email.ts`). `src/instance.ts` holds the write side god mode drives.

"Invite only" means the address has a pending `team_invite` that has not expired
(`hasPendingInvite`). An invite expires `inviteTtlDays` after it was created (7 by default, 0 for
never, at most 3650). `inviteValidSince` computes the cutoff from the current setting on every
read, so a change applies to existing invites: a shorter lifetime expires them, and a longer one
or 0 brings expired ones back. An expired invite does not admit its address at the registration
gate and cannot be accepted. A new invite for the same address to the same team or project
replaces it. While the invite is live, a new one gets 409 `INVITE_ALREADY_PENDING`.

Invites are created and revoked inside a team or one of its projects, so `team_invite` is the
only invite table. God mode's invite settings are `inviteTtlDays` and `inviteSearch`.

`hooks.before` runs the registration gate on `/sign-up/email` (see "Registration gate"). While
verification is required it also holds back `/sign-in/email` and `/sign-in/username`: an existing
account with an unconfirmed address gets 403 `EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED`, better-auth's own code for it.
The check runs before the password is compared, so a wrong password gets the same answer. It
also applies to accounts made before the setting was turned on. It covers password sign-in only:
a magic link confirms the address itself, and a Google or OIDC sign-in is not held back.
`authError` in `features/auth/services` maps that code, and the sign-in form then offers the
confirmation link again when an address was typed. A deactivated account and a disabled password
form are 403s too, so the form goes by the code.

The requirement needs a mail provider: the api refuses to turn it on without one, and
`setEmailSettings` clears it when the provider is removed. So the gate, the sign-up endpoint and
the public `/auth-config` read the setting alone. `magicLink` is refused and cleared the same way,
so the magic-link sender reads only the setting. `/auth-config` answers it as the setting and the
provider together.

`emailAndPassword.requireEmailVerification` is a getter over a module variable that
`hooks.before` refreshes from the setting on every password endpoint. better-auth reads the
option off the options object when `/sign-up/email` decides whether to open a session, so this is
what makes a required confirmation answer sign-up with `token: null` and no cookie instead of a
working session.

Authentication email (`src/mail.ts`) goes out through `@repo/mailer` and is best effort: with no
provider configured, or when the provider rejects the message, it logs and returns false, and the
endpoint answers as if the mail went out. Three kinds are sent: password reset, address
confirmation, and the magic link. Each goes out in the language the address saved, or the
browser's while it has none. God edits the texts and the layout at `/god/email-templates`. The
handler runs on the API origin, so the web app passes
`callbackURL`, `redirectTo` and, for a magic link, `errorCallbackURL` in `features/auth/services`.
The session confirmation on the Security page sends its own magic link from
`features/account/hooks/useConfirmSession.ts`.

With confirmation required, sign-up opens no session. A new address gets its user back. An address
that already has an account gets a made-up user, the same `token: null` and no mail, so the answer
does not reveal that the address is taken. The web sign-up shows a "confirm your email" screen for
both instead of entering the app, and the link opens the session (`autoSignInAfterVerification`).

## Rate limits on sign-in

better-auth limits requests per client address in production, in memory, so each api replica
counts on its own. `rateLimit.customRules` (`authRateLimitRules` in `src/index.ts`) gives the
paths of its own rules a maximum from the auth settings, read per request, and keeps their
window: `signInRateLimit` for `/sign-in/*`, `/sign-up/*`, `/change-password*` and `/change-email*`
per 10 seconds, `emailRateLimit` for `/request-password-reset` and `/send-verification-email` per
minute, `magicLinkRateLimit` for `/sign-in/magic-link*` and `/magic-link/verify*` per minute.
The first matching key wins, so the magic link paths come before `/sign-in/*`. better-auth's `*`
does not cross a `/`. The defaults are
better-auth's (3, 3, 5) and the api takes 1 to 1000, so no limit can be turned off. Every other
auth path keeps better-auth's 100 requests per 10 seconds. An API key never reaches these: its
session is resolved in-process, not through the auth handler.

## Username

The `username()` plugin adds `username` / `display_username` to the user table and the
`/sign-in/username` endpoint. Nobody is asked for a name: `databaseHooks.user.create.before` calls
`generateUsername`, which takes the local part of the address in lower case, removes everything
the plugin's validator rejects, cuts it to 27 characters and uses `user` when nothing is left. It
appends three random digits when that name is taken or is shorter than the 3-character minimum.
SCIM calls `generateUsername` too, since its direct insert passes no hook. An agent's bot user is
a direct insert that sets no username, so its username stays NULL.

The owner changes the name afterwards through `updateUser`. The plugin checks it against other
accounts on `/update-user` and `/sign-up/email`.

A username also addresses an agent in a mention, and a mention is resolved against the project's
members and its agents at once, so the two share one namespace. A member's name must differ from
every agent's on the instance, and an agent's from every member's. Agents of different teams may
share a handle (`ai_agent_team_username_uq`). Every path that sets a member's name checks it
against `ai_agent`: `hooks.before` refuses an `/update-user` that takes a name an agent already
uses, `databaseHooks.user.create.before` refuses a sign-up that carried one, and
`generateUsername` skips such a name. The check for the other direction is in the api, where an
agent is created or renamed.

The plugin's `/is-username-available` takes no session, so it is in `disabledPaths` and answers
404.

The sign-in screen has one field for both identifiers and picks the endpoint by whether what was
typed contains an "@". The verification gate in `hooks.before` runs before the plugin's own check
of `emailAndPassword.requireEmailVerification`.

## Generic OIDC

One OIDC/OAuth2 provider, discovered from the well-known document the operator points it at in god
mode (`app_secret` key `auth.oidc`). It is a social provider with the id `OIDC_PROVIDER_ID`
(`"oidc"`): sign-in is `/sign-in/social` with that provider, the callback is `/callback/oidc`, and
it reuses the `account` table, so it adds none.

A provider per workspace is not built on this one. A sign-in through it joins the account that
already holds the address, which is safe only because the provider is the instance owner's: a
workspace owner's provider could name any address. A per-workspace provider needs the workspace
to prove it owns the address's domain first, and is not part of this repository.

`providerId` is a constant because it is what the `account` rows store, and the rows hold the OIDC
`sub` (`accountSubject`). genericOAuth reads the discovery document once, when its plugin starts,
while this provider changes in god mode without a restart. So better-auth holds a proxy
(`oidcProvider`, registered by the `instanceOidc` plugin), and `refreshOidcProvider()` in
`hooks.before` builds the real provider with genericOAuth from the stored settings whenever they
change, on both halves of the round trip. When the provider is off or incomplete, the request is
refused with `OIDC_DISABLED`.

The redirect URI registered with the identity provider is `OIDC_REDIRECT_URI`,
`/api/auth/oauth2/callback/oidc`. The api passes that path on to better-auth's
`/api/auth/callback/oidc`, so the URI the identity providers hold stays valid.

Signing out leaves the session at the identity provider alone (`disableProviderLogout`). No screen
offers linking an OIDC identity to the signed-in account, so `hooks.before` refuses `/link-social`
for it. Only the standard `email_verified` claim says the address is verified: the OIDC
`mapProfileToUser` reads `true` and `"true"` as verified and anything else, `"false"` included, as
not.

## Turning password authentication off

`AuthSettings.emailPassword` (default `true`). When it is off, `hooks.before` refuses every path in
`PASSWORD_PATHS` with 403 `PASSWORD_AUTH_DISABLED`: the two sign-in endpoints, sign-up, password
reset, and both halves of the magic link, so a magic link issued before the setting changed cannot
be redeemed. Passkeys stay available: a passkey is only ever added to an account that already
exists. A confirmation link is not covered: `/send-verification-email` and `/verify-email` stay
open, and `autoSignInAfterVerification` opens a session for an unconfirmed account.

The setting is read per request. `emailAndPassword.enabled` cannot do this job: better-auth reads
it only on `/sign-up/email` and `/sign-in/email`, so `/sign-in/username`, password reset and the
magic link would stay open. `disabledPaths` is a static array.

The api refuses to turn it off while neither Google nor OIDC is usable, and refuses to make the
last usable provider unusable while it is off (`assertUsableSignInMethod`). Usable means the
provider is enabled with its credentials stored, plus a discovery URL for OIDC. Neither check
contacts the provider, so a wrong secret or a discovery URL that does not answer passes it, and
sign-in then fails.

## Passkey

`passkey({ rpID, rpName, origin })` adds WebAuthn. `rpID` is the hostname the credential binds to:
the host of the first `APP_URL` entry, or `PASSKEY_RP_ID` when it is set. `rpName` is
`PASSKEY_RP_NAME`, "It's a Plan" by default. The compose files and the Helm chart pass neither
variable to the api. `origin` is the whole `APP_URL` list, because the WebAuthn ceremony runs in
the frontend JS. The plugin adds the `passkey` table, which is mapped in the drizzle adapter's
`schema`. localhost is a secure context, so passkeys work over http in dev.

## Google sign-in

The credentials are stored in the database (`app_secret` key `auth.google`, encrypted), so god mode
can change them without a restart.

`socialProviders.google` is a factory that returns the module-level `googleOptions` object.
better-auth builds the provider list once per process, on first use, but the provider keeps that
object by reference and reads `clientId` / `clientSecret` off it on every call. So
`refreshGoogleOptions()` in `hooks.before` reloads it on `/sign-in/social`, `/link-social` and
`/callback/google`, and refuses the request when the credentials are missing or the toggle is off.

By default a provider address that has an account but no link to that identity signs into the
account only when the provider reports the address verified and the account's email is confirmed.
Otherwise the callback redirects with `account_not_linked`. The `trustProviderEmails` instance
setting drops both conditions: `resolveTrustedProviders` then names Google and the OIDC provider,
and `requireLocalEmailVerified` reads false.

## Registration gate

`assertRegistrationAllowed` runs in two places. `hooks.before` runs it on `/sign-up/email`, and
`databaseHooks.user.create.before` runs it for every account better-auth creates, which is what
applies closed/invite-only to a Google, OIDC or magic-link sign-up. SCIM accounts and agent bot
users are written with a direct insert and never reach it.

It refuses with 403 and `REGISTRATION_CLOSED` on a closed instance, `EMAIL_DOMAIN_NOT_ALLOWED` when
the address is not at one of `allowedEmailDomains` (an empty list admits any), and on an invite-only
instance `INVITE_ONLY` when the address has no pending invite and `INVITE_EXPIRED` when its only
invites have expired. The domain check runs first, so an invited address outside the list gets
`EMAIL_DOMAIN_NOT_ALLOWED`.

`INVITE_EXPIRED` reveals that the address was invited, so it is given only in the create hook,
where a provider or a magic link has proven the address. The hook treats any provider as proof and
does not read `email_verified`. The email form, open to anyone, gets `INVITE_ONLY`. The `APIError`s
carry a `code` because the provider callback and the magic link turn that into the `?error=` they
redirect with; without one the callback fails the request instead.
`registration-refusal-redirect.test.ts` pins that redirect, and `invite-forms.test.ts` pins
`INVITE_EXPIRED` on a magic link and `INVITE_ONLY` on the email form.

A domain in `allowedEmailDomains` matches the part of the address after the "@" exactly, so a
subdomain is listed on its own. The list applies to new accounts only. The api also refuses to
invite an address that has no account and is outside it, since it could not register. The gate asks
`registrationEmailAllowed`, which checks the list unless a build installs its own policy with
`setRegistrationEmailPolicy`.

## API keys

`apiKey({ enableSessionForAPIKeys: true })` makes an `x-api-key` header resolve to the owner's
session, so a key is a full-account credential. It therefore expires:
`keyExpiration.defaultExpiresIn` is 90 days and `maxExpiresIn` is a year, and the create dialog in
the web app offers 30/90/180/365 days. The plugin's option is documented as milliseconds but its
handler passes the value to `getDate(value, "sec")`, so `API_KEY_DEFAULT_EXPIRES_IN_SEC` is in
seconds. `maxExpiresIn` is in days, as the plugin reads it. The plugin treats a NULL `expires_at` as
no expiry. No migration sets one, so a personal key made before v1.0.0 works until its owner
deletes it.

The plugin resolves a key to the owner's session on every better-auth endpoint, and what that
session sets up there stays after the key is gone: a passkey enrolled with it signs in after the key
is deleted and the password reset, and a new key renews the expiry. So the first check in
`hooks.before` refuses any request that carries an `x-api-key` header: a key is for the planner API,
and the account is managed from a signed-in session. The connected-apps routes refuse a key too. The
check reads `ctx.request`, which a server-side `auth.api.*` call does not carry, so `issueKey` and
`getSessionFromHeaders` are unaffected. `hooks.before` also refuses an `/api-key/update` that carries
`expiresIn`: a longer life is a new key.

An agent's key carries no expiry. An agent replays its stored secret with nothing that would renew
it, and an external agent's operator rotates it through `regenerate-key`. The plugin applies the
default to every key it creates, so `issueKey` in `apps/api/src/modules/agents/core/service.ts`
clears `expires_at` on the row afterwards.

A key the plugin refuses with a 401 or 403 (expired, disabled, unknown or malformed) makes it throw
out of `auth.api.getSession` rather than return no session. `getSessionFromHeaders` turns that into
"no session", so an expired key is answered with a 401 instead of a 500. It rethrows any other
refusal.

The plugin's rate limit is off (`rateLimit.enabled: false`). It restarts its window only after a
pause longer than the window, and it counts every `getSession`, of which an MCP tool call makes two.
The off switch also skips the limits each older key stored in its own row. apps/api limits keys
instead: `requestUser` in `shared/auth-context.ts` counts each request made with a key in
`shared/key-rate-limit.ts`, one fixed one-minute window per key. The limit is
`requestsPerMinute` in god mode (General → API keys, `app_setting` key `apiKeys`), 1200 by
default, 0 for none. Each api process keeps the setting for a minute (`keptApiKeySettings`): a
change saved in god mode applies at once on the replica that saved it and within a minute on the
others. A key over it gets 429 `RATE_LIMITED` with a `Retry-After` header, and an MCP
tool call dispatched by an internal agent returns that as `retryAfterSeconds`. `POST /mcp` counts
each JSON-RPC message of the request, a batch included, and answers 429 itself. The tool calls it
dispatches are not counted again: `requestUser` recognises them by `getMcpClientRequest`, an
in-process link a client cannot set. The windows are kept in memory, so each api replica counts
on its own.

## MCP OAuth

`mcp()` from `@better-auth/mcp` serves OAuth 2.1 to MCP clients, with `jwt()` signing the access
tokens. A client that requests a token without the `resource` parameter gets an opaque token, which
`/mcp` refuses. `mcp()` adds the `oauth_client`, `oauth_resource`, `oauth_client_resource`,
`oauth_refresh_token`, `oauth_access_token`, `oauth_consent` and `oauth_client_assertion` tables,
and `jwt()` adds `jwks`. `mcp()` writes the MCP resource (`<API_URL>/mcp`) into `oauth_resource`
when the auth instance is created, on its first use, and leaves an existing row as it is. Any client
registers itself (RFC 7591), as ChatGPT and Claude do. The provider asks the person for consent the
first time a client asks for their account. Only `authorization_code` and `refresh_token` are
granted, so every token acts for a person. A registration that also lists a grant the server does
not issue, as Claude's connector does with `jwt-bearer`, is registered with the supported grants.
One that lists none of them is refused.

MCP clients register without `application_type`, and `mcp()` infers it
(`clientRegistrationDefaultApplicationType: 'infer'`): a client whose callback is http on
`localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]` (Claude Code) or uses a custom scheme such as Cursor's
`cursor://` is registered as `native`, and any other as `web`, which takes an https callback only.
better-auth's own default, `web`, refuses the first two. A client that sends its `application_type`
keeps it.

The issuer is `API_URL` itself, path included, so the tokens and the discovery documents name the
URL a client reaches. The api serves the documents at the root of its origin
(`oauthAuthorizationServerMetadata`, `openIdConfiguration`, `oauthProtectedResourceMetadata`), and
the endpoints in them get the path back the way the links in auth emails do.

`verifyMcpAccessToken` checks a token against the instance's own keys in-process, with `iss` set to
`API_URL` and `aud` to `<API_URL>/mcp`, so changing `API_URL` ends every issued token. It refuses a
DPoP-bound token (`cnf` claim), because it takes no proof. Then it reads what a JWT cannot carry:

- The account must not be deactivated. This ends every MCP token of the account at once, whichever
  way it was deactivated. God mode also deletes the account's sessions and OAuth tokens. SCIM only
  sets `user.active`.
- A token issued in a session ends with that session, as better-auth's introspection has it.
  Signing out does not disconnect a client: deleting a session sets `session_id` on its refresh
  tokens to NULL, and a token refreshed after that carries no `sid`.
- The token's client must still be connected to the account, through the person's consent or a
  refresh token that is neither revoked nor expired. Disconnecting it on the account's Security page
  (`DELETE /account/connected-apps/:clientId`) deletes the consent, the refresh tokens, the
  `oauth_access_token` rows and any pending authorization code, which would otherwise connect the
  client again. This ends its tokens at once.

better-auth accepts a plain-HTTP MCP resource only on a loopback host, so any other instance without
HTTPS leaves `mcp()` and `jwt()` out and serves MCP to API keys only.

## OpenAPI reference

The `openAPI()` plugin (`better-auth/plugins`) documents the auth handler. It serves a Scalar UI at
`/api/auth/reference` and the raw schema at `/api/auth/open-api/generate-schema`. The schema is built
from every active plugin, so the passkey and apiKey endpoints appear without any manual description.
This is separate from the planner's own OpenAPI docs at `/docs` (the `@elysiajs/swagger` spec, which
does not see the catch-all auth handler).

God mode picks who may read both references and their raw documents (General → API docs). The api
answers 401 without a session and 403 to a user outside that audience. The web page loads `/docs/json`
with the session and hands it to Scalar.

# The revision engine

Two people have the same board open. One of them drags a card to another column. The other one
sees it move a few seconds later, without touching anything.

That is what this engine does. Every screen that has to stay current watches a **scope**, the
engine keeps a counter per scope, and the screen refetches its data when its counter changes.

## Walking through one change

Say someone renames issue 450, which lives in project 12.

1. The API updates the row. A trigger on the `issue` table runs and increments two counters in
   the `revision` table: `board:12` and `issue:450`.
2. Meanwhile every open tab asks the API, every 8 seconds, for the counters it cares about:

   ```
   GET /sync/rev?scopes=board:12,issue:450,inbox:12
   { "revs": { "board:12": "38", "issue:450": "13", "inbox:12": "5" } }
   ```

3. A tab showing the board had `board:12` at `37`, now reads `38`, and refetches the board
   issues. A tab with issue 450 open refetches the issue and its comments. A tab looking at a
   different project asked for none of this and refetches nothing.

The counter has no meaning beyond "different from last time". Clients compare it for equality
and never do arithmetic on it, so gaps in the numbers are harmless.

## Scopes

| Scope                        | Watched by                    | Moves when                                                        |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `board:<projectId>`          | the work items board          | any issue, label, relation, initiative or cycle in the project changes |
| `issue:<issueId>`            | the issue screen              | the issue, its comments, checklists, attachments or field values change |
| `initiative:<initiativeId>`  | the initiative screen         | the initiative or any issue inside it changes                     |
| `inbox:<projectId>:<userId>` | the inbox                     | that user gets a notification, reads one, or deletes one          |
| `inbox:all`                  | the app icon badge, desktop notifications | any `inbox:<projectId>:<userId>` of a project the user can read moves, or such a project is gained or lost |

Comments deliberately do not move the board: the board does not show them, so refetching it
would be wasted work.

The inbox is the one scope that belongs to a person rather than an entity. Clients ask for
`inbox:12` and the API fills in the session user, so one person can never watch another's inbox.

`inbox:all` has no row of its own. The API reads the session user's inbox row of every project
they can read and answers with the list of `<projectId>=<rev>` pairs, so the badge watches one
scope however many projects the user sees. A sum of the counters would be shorter, but it can
come back to an earlier value when a project is lost while another inbox moves.

## Where the code lives

| File                                   | What it holds                                            |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/db/drizzle/0070_*.sql`       | `bump_rev`, the trigger functions, and their triggers    |
| `apps/api/src/modules/sync/service.ts` | the scope names and the read queries                     |
| `apps/api/src/modules/sync/index.ts`   | `GET /sync/rev`                                          |
| `apps/web/src/context/syncContext.tsx` | the one poll every screen shares                         |
| `apps/web/src/hooks/useLiveRefresh.ts` | what a screen calls                                      |
| `apps/web/src/utils/revScopes.ts`      | the scope names on the client                            |

Nothing in the application writes a counter. The triggers do, which means a write from the
worker, the bot, an MCP tool or a hand-typed `UPDATE` in psql moves the marker as surely as a
write from the API.

## Using it in a screen

```ts
useLiveRefresh({
  scope: revScope.issue(issueId),
  targets: [qk.issue(issueId), qk.feed(issueId)],
});
```

That is the whole integration. No screen runs its own timer: `SyncProvider` collects the scopes
of everything currently mounted, asks for them in one request, and invalidates the targets of
the scopes that moved. The API takes at most 20 scopes per request; `getRevs` splits a longer
list into requests of 20 and merges the answers. The poll stops while nothing is registered.
While the tab sits in the background it covers only the scopes of watchers that pass
`background: true`, and stops when there are none. Desktop notifications pass it while they
are on, so a hidden tab still reads the inbox marker while its other screens stay paused.

## Reading the counters

```sql
select r.scope, r.rev, m.role, pr.permissions
from revision r
join project_member m on m.project_id = r.project_id and m.user_id = $userId
left join team_role pr on pr.id = m.role_id
where r.scope = any($scopes)
```

The join is also the access check. Ask for a project you are not a member of and no row comes
back, so the answer is `"0"`, exactly what a scope that has never changed returns. The role
decides the rest: each scope kind names a resource (`work_items` for the board and an issue,
`initiatives` for an initiative), and a member whose role may not read it gets the same `"0"`.
The inbox names no resource — it is the caller's own.

A new scope therefore needs a correct `project_id` on the row and the resource its watchers must
be allowed to read.

## Adding a table to an existing scope

One line in a migration. Say reactions on issues get their own table:

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER issue_reaction_rev AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON issue_reaction
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION rev_issue_child('issue_id', 'detail');
```

The first argument is the column holding the issue id. The second says who shows the change:
`board` if the board does, `detail` if only the issue screen does. The issue screen already
watches `issue:<id>`, so reactions start arriving with no client change at all.

A table that reaches its owner through another table needs its own function next to the ones in
the migration. `rev_checklist_item()` is the example to copy: it goes from
`issue_checklist_item` to `issue_checklist` to `issue`.

## Adding a new scope

A new kind of scope touches two more places: the entry in `scopeKind` in
`apps/api/src/modules/sync/service.ts`, which names it, makes the API accept it, and says which resource a
watcher must be allowed to read, and the mirror in `apps/web/src/utils/revScopes.ts`.
`packages/db/AGENTS.md` keeps the same recipe next to the schema.

## Four rules before you touch the triggers

**Take the scopes in one order everywhere: board, then issue, then initiative.** Opposite orders
deadlock. Two counters of the same kind — the initiatives an issue moved between — go in id
order, for the same reason.

**`revision.project_id` has no foreign key on purpose.** Deleting a project cascades into its
issues, and each of those deletes inserts a counter row for a project on its way out — a foreign
key would abort the delete. A deferred constraint trigger on `project` removes the leftovers at
commit, after the cascades.

**A child trigger does nothing when its issue is already gone.** Its rows cascade away after the
issue and can no longer resolve a project; the issue's own delete already moved the board counter
and dropped `issue:<id>`.

**Bulk writes bump a counter many times, and that is fine.** Nobody reads the value, only the
change.

## Why it works this way

**A counter, not a log of changes.** The client only needs to know that something changed.
Answering "what changed since revision X" would mean commit-ordering guarantees (`xid8` with
`pg_snapshot_xmin`), soft deletes, and patch application in the browser. The marker is opaque, so
that can still be added later.

**Triggers, not calls from the application.** A counter cannot be forgotten in a new code path,
and writes that never pass through the API still move it.

**Polling, not a push stream.** `NOTIFY` takes a lock on every commit that carries one, which
serializes all transactions on the instance; it stops working behind PgBouncer in transaction
pooling mode, and drops notifications on a broken connection, so a poll would be needed anyway.
One small request per tab every 8 seconds is cheap enough.

# @repo/agent-tools

Custom tools for AI agents: external services (Jina, Firecrawl, Telegram) an agent
can call at runtime. Each service is an _integration_ that owns a credential and
exposes one or more _tools_.

## Model

- **Integration**: an external service. Holds a `credentialSchema` (the fields a
  human fills once per credential, such as an API key) and a list of tools.
- **Tool**: one callable action. Declares an `inputSchema` (what the model passes at
  call time) and an `execute` that runs it with the decrypted credential.

A team can store several credentials per integration, and a configured tool binds
one tool to one credential. That way two Jina keys can back two copies of the same
tool.

## Add a tool to an existing integration

You only touch that integration's folder.

1. Create `src/tools/<integration>/<action>.ts`:

   ```ts
   import { z } from "zod";
   import type { CustomToolEntry } from "../../types";
   import { jsonOrThrow } from "../../http";

   export const telegramFoo: CustomToolEntry = {
     key: "telegram_foo",          // unique across ALL integrations
     label: "Telegram Foo",
     description: "What the tool does. Passed to the model verbatim.",
     inputSchema: z.object({
       text: z.string().min(1).describe("Field docs help the model."),
     }),
     execute: async (credential, input) => {
       const res = await fetch("https://api.telegram.org/...", { ... });
       return await jsonOrThrow(res, "Telegram foo");
     },
   };
   ```

2. Add it to the `tools` array in `src/tools/<integration>/index.ts`.

That's it. The registry indexes it, the API catalog exposes it, and the runtime
resolves it.

## Add a new integration

1. Create `src/tools/<name>/`:
   - one file per tool (`CustomToolEntry`, as above);
   - `index.ts` exporting the `Integration`:

     ```ts
     import type { Integration } from '../../types';
     import { myToolA } from './a';

     export const myService: Integration = {
       key: 'my_service',
       label: 'My Service',
       credentialSchema: [{ key: 'apiKey', label: 'API key', type: 'secret', required: true }],
       tools: [myToolA],
     };
     ```

   Optional fields of the `Integration`:
   - `icon`: the brand mark in `icon.ts`, one SVG path in a 24×24 box and its fill
     color. Leave the color out for a black mark, so it follows the text color.
     Without an icon the interface shows the label's first letters.
   - `website`: the service's homepage, linked from the interface.
   - `verify`: asks the service whether it accepts a credential before it is saved, in
     `verify.ts`. Use one request that spends nothing. Answer `rejected` only for a
     refusal the API itself sends (a bot wall answers 403 with a page). Answer
     `unavailable` for anything else that is not a success. Call an address that comes
     from the credential through `pinnedFetch` from `@repo/net`. Without `verify` the
     credential is saved unchecked.
   - `credentialOptional`: its tools also run with no credential, on the service's
     keyless tier.
   - `help` on a credential field: markdown shown behind a "?" by the field's label.

2. Register it in `src/registry.ts`. This is the one manual step: import the
   integration and add it to the `INTEGRATIONS` array.

Everything downstream reads from that array: the tool index, the
`integrationDescriptors()` catalog for the UI, and `coerceConfig`/`redactConfig`. No
other file needs editing.

## Integrations from outside this package

A build that extends the api adds integrations of its own at startup with
`setExtraIntegrations([...])`. They join the core's in the tool index and the catalog.
Each call replaces the previous ones, and a call without an argument removes them. A
key that is already taken throws. A configured tool whose integration is removed stays
stored, and the runtime skips it.

## An integration without a credential

An integration whose tools need no account with an external service (PDF downloads
the file and parses it in the api process) declares `credentialSchema: []`. Its tools are configured without a
credential, its `execute` receives `{}`, and the API refuses to store a credential for
it.

## Rules

- **A tool `key` is unique across all integrations.** The tool index is a flat map by
  key; a duplicate throws when `registry.ts` loads or when `setExtraIntegrations` adds it.
- **Mark secrets `type: "secret"`** in `credentialSchema`. Non-secret fields are
  stored in plaintext and shown unredacted in the list UI.
- **Throw a clear `Error` on failure.** The runtime catches it and returns
  `{ error: message }` to the model instead of aborting the run, so that message is
  the model's only signal. Use `jsonOrThrow` from `http.ts` for fetch calls.
- **`execute` receives the decrypted credential**, keyed by `credentialSchema` field
  key. Read config values off it; the model never sees the secret.

## Config field types

`string`, `secret`, `url`, `number`, `boolean`. `coerceConfig` validates and coerces
submitted values against the schema; a missing required field returns a 400.

# @repo/auth

The server-side better-auth instance, consumed by `apps/api`. `docs/dev/auth.md` explains how each
sign-in method, setting and token works. Read it before you change one.

## Rules

- This package is server-only. Never import a client SDK (`better-auth/react`) here.
- A change to plugins or fields can change the DB tables. Run `bun run auth:generate`, then
  `db:generate` and `db:migrate`. `src/schema/auth.ts` in `@repo/db` is generated.
- `API_URL` and `APP_URL` are mandatory. Do not add a localhost fallback: cookies, the passkey
  relying party and every link in an auth email come from them, so a wrong value fails silently.
- Instance settings are in the database so they change without a restart. Read them through
  `src/instance.ts`. Never inline a query on `app_setting` or `app_secret`. Secrets never leave the
  server.
- Do not replace the `emailAndPassword.requireEmailVerification` getter with a static value: `true`
  locks every account out, `false` hands an unconfirmed sign-up a session.
- Do not reassign `googleOptions`. Assign its fields: the provider keeps the object by reference.
- Keep `accountLinking.trustedProviders` as `resolveTrustedProviders`. It trusts a provider only
  while `trustProviderEmails` is on. A static list would let whoever registered an address first
  receive its real owner.
- Password sign-in off is read per request, so it cannot be `emailAndPassword.enabled: false` or a
  `disabledPaths` entry.
- Use `getSessionFromHeaders`, not `auth.api.getSession`, where a request may carry a key. An
  expired key throws out of `getSession` and would answer 500.
- A key is for the planner API. `hooks.before` refuses `x-api-key` on every auth endpoint. Only an
  agent's key has no expiry (`issueKey`).
- Every auth email link carries a `callbackURL` or `redirectTo` on the **web** origin. Without one
  it lands on the API, which renders nothing.
- A username shares one namespace with agents. Every path that sets a member's name checks it
  against `ai_agent`.
- `/is-username-available` stays in `disabledPaths`: it would tell a stranger which addresses are
  registered.
- Invites belong to a team. There is no instance-level invite table. Do not add a god mode invite
  section.
- An OIDC provider per workspace is not built on the instance provider: a workspace owner's
  provider could name any address.
- **`API_URL` with a path:** better-auth's `baseURL` gets only the origin. Every public URL built
  from it gets the path back through `apiPublicUrl` / `withPublicOrigin`.
- **Cookies:** `sameSite: "lax"`. If frontend and backend run on different domains, switch to
  `sameSite: "none"` + `secure: true`.

# @repo/db

Drizzle ORM + `postgres-js` over PostgreSQL. The source of truth for the DB schema.

## Structure

- `src/schema/auth.ts` is **generated** by better-auth. Do not edit it; run `bun run auth:generate`.
- `src/schema/app.ts`: hand-written application tables. Add domain tables here.
- `src/schema/scim.ts`: hand-written SCIM tables.
- `drizzle.config.ts` reads only `src/schema/index.ts`. Export a new schema file from it.
- `src/permissions.ts`: the permission matrix stored in `team_role.permissions`.
- `src/settings.ts` / `src/secrets.ts`: instance config, `app_setting` in plaintext jsonb,
  `app_secret` encrypted with `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.
- `src/domains/`: a new config that several processes read gets a module here: shape, defaults and
  a reader that decrypts it if it is encrypted. A config only one process reads stays out. The
  caller keeps writes and validation. `storage.ts` also holds the upload check and quota queries.
- `src/migrate.ts`: programmatic migrator, no drizzle-kit in prod.

## Workflow

1. Edit `schema/app.ts` or `schema/scim.ts`, or regenerate `schema/auth.ts`.
2. `bun run db:generate`, which writes SQL to `drizzle/`.
3. `bun run db:migrate`, then `bun run db:migrate:test` for the test DB.

Never `drizzle-kit push`. Every schema change goes through a committed migration.

## Conventions

- Explicit snake_case column names (`text("created_at")`). No `casing` option.
- New FK: `onDelete: "cascade"` if the row cannot exist without its parent, `onDelete: "set null"`
  for an optional link (assignee, author, cycle, parent issue). Keep `cascade` on a nullable FK when
  NULL has its own meaning (system role, public board) or a CHECK needs the owner.
- Agents are enumerated through `ai_agent`; `user` has no non-human flag. See `docs/dev/agents.md`.

## Revision triggers

Triggers write `revision`; application code leaves it alone. The one exception is `appendRunEvents`,
which calls `bump_rev` because `agent_run_trace` has no trigger.

To make a table move an existing scope, add one line to a migration:

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER issue_cycle_rev AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON issue_cycle
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION rev_issue_child('issue_id', 'detail');
```

For a new table, append the line to the SQL that `db:generate` writes. For an existing table
`db:generate` writes nothing, so run `bunx drizzle-kit generate --custom --name=<name>` in
`packages/db`: the migrator runs only files listed in the journal.

`rev_issue_child` takes the column holding the issue id, and `board` or `detail`. Both move the
issue and its initiative; `board` also moves the board. Any other value acts as `detail`. Tables
owned by an initiative use `rev_initiative_child('initiative_id')`, and tables with a `document_id`
column use `rev_document_child()`.

A table that reaches its owner another way gets its own function in a new migration, modelled on
`rev_checklist_item` in `0070_revision_triggers.sql`. A later migration can replace a function: the
current `rev_issue` is in `0142_issue_key_alias.sql`.

Inside a function, keep the lock order: board, then issue, then initiative, two of one kind in id
order, with `documents` before issue and initiative. It stops two single-row writes from
deadlocking. `inbox` and `runner-queue` are outside the order: each is taken alone.

A new scope kind also needs its entry in `scopeKind` in `apps/api/src/modules/sync/service.ts`, its
name in `apps/api/src/modules/sync/model.ts` and the mirror in `apps/web/src/utils/revScopes.ts`. A
scope across projects has no `scopeKind` entry: `apps/api/src/modules/sync/index.ts` handles it.
